prompt: Implement count_even(values: list[int]) -> int. Return how many values are even, make one pass, and do not mutate the input. State the time and extra-space complexity after coding.
hints: An empty list should contribute zero; each item needs one parity check.
Accumulate a count while iterating once.
tests:
assert count_even([]) == 0, "empty input should count zero"
assert count_even([1, 2, 4, 5]) == 2, "mixed parity count"
assert count_even([-2, 0, 3]) == 2, "negative and zero are handled"

prompt: BUILD QUEST: For an ascending list, implement linear_contains(values, target), binary_contains(values, target), and search_report(values, target). The first two return booleans; the report returns a dict with keys linear and binary. Keep the input unchanged and explain why the two helpers have different time complexity. This is intentionally a multi-function quest.
hints: The linear helper can stop at the first match; the binary helper maintains an inclusive left/right window.
When the target is smaller than the middle value, discard the right half; when larger, discard the left half.
The report should call both helpers rather than duplicate their search logic.
tests:
data = [-5, -1, 0, 3, 9]
assert linear_contains(data, -5) is True, "linear finds first item"
assert binary_contains(data, 9) is True, "binary finds last item"
assert search_report(data, 4) == {"linear": False, "binary": False}, "both reject a missing item"
assert search_report([], 0) == {"linear": False, "binary": False}, "empty input is safe"
assert data == [-5, -1, 0, 3, 9], "searches must not mutate input"

prompt: A function visits each of n items exactly once and performs constant work per item. Which time-growth class describes it?
hints: Count how the work changes when n doubles.
One visit per item grows in direct proportion to n.

prompt: Two independent loops each may visit all n items. What is the tightest usual time-growth class for the combined code?
hints: Sequential loops add their work; nested loops multiply it.
Two n-sized loops run one after another, so 2n drops its constant factor.

prompt: Implement is_palindrome(text: str) -> bool. Compare from both ends, ignoring case and non-alphanumeric characters. Return True for an empty or punctuation-only string.
hints: Move left and right toward the center after skipping characters that are not letters or digits.
Compare lowercase forms; a mismatch can return False immediately.
tests:
assert is_palindrome("") is True, "empty text is a palindrome"
assert is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama") is True, "normalized phrase"
assert is_palindrome("race a car") is False, "non-palindrome phrase"
assert is_palindrome(" !!! " ) is True, "punctuation-only text has no mismatch"

prompt: Fix the merge routine: implement merge_sorted(left, right) -> list[int] for two ascending lists. Return a new ascending list, preserving duplicates and all values. Use one pointer per input and handle either list becoming empty.
hints: At each step append the smaller current head, then advance only that pointer.
When one pointer reaches the end, append the remaining tail from the other list.
tests:
assert merge_sorted([], []) == [], "two empty lists"
assert merge_sorted([], [-2, 4]) == [-2, 4], "empty left tail"
assert merge_sorted([1, 3, 3], [2, 3, 5]) == [1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5], "duplicates stay in order"
left = [0, 2]
right = [1]
assert merge_sorted(left, right) == [0, 1, 2], "interleaved values"
assert left == [0, 2] and right == [1], "inputs are not mutated"

prompt: Implement remove_duplicates_sorted(values: list[int]) -> int. The input is ascending. Compact unique values at the front in place and return the number of unique values; the suffix after that length does not matter.
hints: Keep a write pointer for the next unseen value and scan with a read pointer.
The first value, when present, is already unique; only write when the value differs from the previous kept value.
tests:
values = []
assert remove_duplicates_sorted(values) == 0 and values == [], "empty list"
values = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
length = remove_duplicates_sorted(values)
assert length == 3 and values[:length] == [1, 2, 3], "mixed duplicates"
values = [0, 0, 0]
length = remove_duplicates_sorted(values)
assert length == 1 and values[:length] == [0], "all values equal"
values = [-2, -2, -1]
length = remove_duplicates_sorted(values)
assert length == 2 and values[:length] == [-2, -1], "negative values"

prompt: Implement first_index(sorted_values: list[int], target: int) -> int. Return the first index containing target in an ascending list with duplicates, or -1 when absent. Use O(log n) search rather than a full scan.
hints: On equality, save the index and continue searching to the left.
Use a half-open or inclusive interval consistently, and stop when no candidates remain.
tests:
assert first_index([], 4) == -1, "empty input"
assert first_index([1, 2, 2, 2, 5], 2) == 1, "leftmost duplicate"
assert first_index([1, 3, 5], 1) == 0, "first position"
assert first_index([1, 3, 5], 4) == -1, "missing target"
assert first_index([1, 3, 5], 9) == -1, "target beyond right boundary"

prompt: Implement search_insert(sorted_values: list[int], target: int) -> int. Return the leftmost index where target is found or inserted in an ascending list. Duplicates insert before existing equal values.
hints: This is a lower-bound search: keep a candidate answer when values[mid] is at least target.
When values[mid] is smaller, move left past mid; otherwise keep mid and move right down.
tests:
assert search_insert([], 3) == 0, "empty list inserts at zero"
assert search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 5) == 2, "existing value"
assert search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 2) == 1, "between values"
assert search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 9) == 4, "after all values"
assert search_insert([1, 2, 2, 4], 2) == 1, "leftmost duplicate position"

prompt: A binary search discards half of its remaining sorted candidates after each comparison. Which time-growth class describes searching n candidates?
hints: Ask how many halvings reduce n to one candidate.
The answer counts the exponent in 2^k ≈ n.

prompt: Implement two_sum(values: list[int], target: int) -> tuple[int, int]. Return indices of the first pair encountered whose values sum to target, using distinct indices; return (-1, -1) when no pair exists. Aim for O(n) average time.
hints: For each value, look up target - value among indices already seen.
Check the complement before storing the current index so one element cannot pair with itself.
tests:
assert two_sum([], 0) == (-1, -1), "empty input has no pair"
assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == (0, 1), "basic complement lookup"
assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == (0, 1), "duplicate values use distinct indices"
assert two_sum([1, 2, 4], 8) == (-1, -1), "missing pair"
assert two_sum([-3, 5, 1], 2) == (0, 1), "negative values"

prompt: Implement first_unique_char(text: str) -> int. Return the index of the first character occurring exactly once, preserving case; return -1 if none exists.
hints: Make one frequency table, then make a second left-to-right pass.
Do not confuse a character's first position with its total frequency.
tests:
assert first_unique_char("") == -1, "empty text"
assert first_unique_char("leetcode") == 0, "first character is unique"
assert first_unique_char("loveleetcode") == 2, "later unique character"
assert first_unique_char("aabb") == -1, "no unique character"
assert first_unique_char("AaA") == 1, "case is preserved"

prompt: Implement group_anagrams(words: list[str]) -> list[list[str]]. Group words with the same letters, preserve input order within each group, and order groups by the first word that created each group. Treat case as significant.
hints: A sorted spelling is a canonical key for an anagram group.
Use a dictionary from key to the group list, and append a group only when its key is new.
tests:
assert group_anagrams([]) == [], "empty input"
assert group_anagrams(["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]) == [["eat", "tea", "ate"], ["tan", "nat"], ["bat"]], "stable anagram groups"
assert group_anagrams(["", ""]) == [["", ""]], "empty strings share a group"
assert group_anagrams(["Ab", "ba"]) == [["Ab"], ["ba"]], "case-sensitive keys"

prompt: Implement is_valid_brackets(text: str) -> bool. Validate (), [], and {} nesting while ignoring every non-bracket character. Return False for a mismatched, prematurely closed, or unclosed bracket.
hints: Push opening brackets; a closing bracket must match the most recent opening bracket.
At the end, the stack must be empty.
tests:
assert is_valid_brackets("") is True, "no brackets are valid"
assert is_valid_brackets("a[(b){c}]") is True, "proper nesting"
assert is_valid_brackets("([)]") is False, "crossed brackets"
assert is_valid_brackets("hello )") is False, "premature close"
assert is_valid_brackets("{[()] }") is True, "spaces are ignored"

prompt: Implement next_greater(values: list[int]) -> list[int]. For each position, return the first later value strictly greater than it, or -1 if none exists. Use a monotonic stack so each item is pushed and popped at most once.
hints: Keep indices whose next greater value has not been seen yet.
When the current value exceeds the value at the stack's top index, resolve that older index and continue popping.
tests:
assert next_greater([]) == [], "empty input"
assert next_greater([2, 1, 2, 4, 3]) == [4, 2, 4, -1, -1], "mixed rises and drops"
assert next_greater([5]) == [-1], "single value"
assert next_greater([2, 2]) == [-1, -1], "equal values are not greater"
assert next_greater([-1, -2, -3]) == [-1, -1, -1], "decreasing negatives"

prompt: Implement shortest_path(graph: dict[str, list[str]], start: str, target: str) -> int for an unweighted directed graph. Return the minimum number of edges from start to target, or -1 if unreachable. Handle cycles and start == target.
hints: Use a queue of (node, distance) pairs and mark a node visited when enqueuing it.
The first time BFS dequeues target, its distance is minimal.

prompt: Implement count_components(n: int, edges: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> int for an undirected graph whose vertices are 0 through n-1. Count isolated vertices, ignore repeated edges, and do not traverse outside the valid vertex range.
hints: Build adjacency lists, then start a DFS/BFS from every still-unvisited vertex.
Mark each vertex before following its neighbors; increment the component count once per new traversal.
tests:
assert count_components(0, []) == 0, "empty graph"
assert count_components(4, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 1)]) == 2, "duplicate edge still one component"
assert count_components(5, [(0, 1), (3, 4)]) == 3, "isolated vertex counts"
assert count_components(3, [(0, 4), (1, 2)]) == 2, "out-of-range edge is ignored"

prompt: Explain when BFS is preferable to DFS for an unweighted graph, why marking nodes when discovered prevents duplicate work, and the time/space complexity of either traversal with adjacency lists. Include one edge case a robust implementation must test.
hints: Contrast shortest-path layers with simply reaching every node.
Name the queue/stack frontier and the visited set in the complexity accounting.
rubric: Says BFS explores in distance layers and therefore finds an unweighted shortest path; DFS does not guarantee that order.
Explains that marking on discovery prevents cycles and repeated enqueues/visits.
Gives O(V+E) time and O(V) auxiliary space for an adjacency-list traversal, plus an edge case such as a cycle, disconnected graph, or start equal to target.

prompt: BOSS: Implement merge_sort(values: list[int]) -> list[int] without mutating the input or calling sort/sorted, and sort_students(students: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> list[tuple[str, int]] ordered by ascending score then ascending name. Explain why merge_sort is O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space, and make the tie-break deterministic.
hints: Split until a list has at most one item, then merge two sorted halves.
For student records compare (score, name); for numeric merge, append the smaller head and then the remaining tail.
Copy records or build new lists so neither input is changed.
tests:
values = [3, -1, 2, 2, 0]
assert merge_sort(values) == [-1, 0, 2, 2, 3], "numeric merge sort"
assert values == [3, -1, 2, 2, 0], "numeric input is unchanged"
assert merge_sort([]) == [], "empty merge sort"
students = [("zoe", 90), ("amy", 80), ("lee", 90), ("bea", 80)]
assert sort_students(students) == [("amy", 80), ("bea", 80), ("lee", 90), ("zoe", 90)], "score then name order"
assert students == [("zoe", 90), ("amy", 80), ("lee", 90), ("bea", 80)], "student input is unchanged"

prompt: What is the usual comparison-based time complexity of merge sort on n items, including its worst case?
hints: There are logarithmically many split levels.
Each level merges a total of n items.

prompt: A binary search halves the candidate range each step. For n = 1024 candidates, what is ceil(log2(n))? Enter the number only.
hints: Compute powers of two until you reach 1024.
2^10 equals 1024.

prompt: Implement top_k_frequent(values: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]. Return up to k distinct values ordered by decreasing frequency, then increasing numeric value for ties. Return [] when k <= 0.
hints: Count values with a dictionary, then make the ranking key (-frequency, value).
Sort the distinct keys by that key and slice to k; never return a duplicate value.
tests:
assert top_k_frequent([], 3) == [], "empty input"
assert top_k_frequent([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2) == [1, 2], "most frequent values"
assert top_k_frequent([4, 1, 3, 2], 3) == [1, 2, 3], "numeric tie-break"
assert top_k_frequent([2, 2, 1], 0) == [], "nonpositive k"
assert top_k_frequent([5, 5, 6], 9) == [5, 6], "k larger than distinct count"
